intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honor all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 263263292: an overconfident wastebasket, launching fireflies. Here's how that became a night at Dobbin's Hollow.

rolls.became: The bin by the taps at Dobbin's Hollow caravan park. Everything anyone throws lands in it, so it's never once missed, so it's sure it never will. It has button eyes, a half-lidded look, and, eventually, a captain's hat nobody gave it.
A bin has a lid, and a lid flips. The bin flicks things out instead of taking them in, which is the whole joke turned inside out.

Fireflies really do rest by day in damp, dark places, and nowhere is damper or darker than the bottom of a bin. One in a tent window at night looks exactly like a light left on. Overripe peaches bring more of them.

Drag from the bin to a dark window and a firefly flies your thread, a strand of glowing yarn, all the way there. The thread has a length (sugar water makes it longer), and you bend it round Dobbin's torch, because anything that flies through the beam ends up in his jam jar.

Mr Dobbin screwed his LIGHTS OUT AT 10 sign to the bin, because it's the only post by the taps. So the bin lights every window in the park, and Dobbin storms out in his tartan dressing gown to shout LIGHTS OUT at caravans with their lights off.

Mr Dobbin, landlord, on his rounds with a torch and a megaphone. He gets in the way, and he's also the payoff: every time he shouts, the campers wake up and talk about it. You even buy him a louder megaphone and stronger coffee, and swap his torch batteries for flat ones.
Dobbin, of Dobbin's Hollow. And, it turns out, D.D.

The things the fireflies turn up in the dark tell a story: a boy's notebook signed D.D., a photo of a kid with a jam jar of fireflies outside his furious father's caravan, a catapult, and his dad's old sign: LIGHTS OUT AT 10. THAT MEANS YOU, DOBBIN. Dobbin the Dreadful grew up to be his dad.

rolls.value: a map you explore and reveal
rolls.became: The park is dark felt. Every flight lights up what it passes over, and that's how you find the tent meadow, caravan row, the yurts in the woods and the clubhouse, and what's lying in the grass. Unlit campers still snore, so you can aim at a Z.

rolls.value: automation you program (an action queue with priorities)
rolls.became: The Clockwork Lid. Pin paths you've flown as standing orders and the lid flicks them again by itself, top of the list first, whenever that window's dark, there's a firefly home and the torch is out of the way. Sticky notes add slots; winding the key makes it faster.

Draw a thread that crosses itself, and the firefly goes round the ring and blinks in time with the window, like the synchronous fireflies of the Smoky Mountains. Twice the gossip. Nothing tells you this, except a nine-year-old's notebook, if you find it.

When all eight billion people on Earth have heard, Dobbin walks to the bin with his jam jar. Take his keys and the bin becomes landlord, while Dobbin flicks fireflies at it from a deck chair. Or hand him the lid, and he lights his own bedroom window and goes to sleep with the light on.

Five parts of the park, each further from the bin, each opened by a longer thread. Campers book the free pitches as word gets round, then squeeze more families in. While you're away, the park keeps talking, more quietly.
The meter is who's heard: pitch 7, the whole park, the village, the county, the country, and then everyone on Earth. Gossip is also what you swap at the taps for peaches, sugar water and megaphones.
A felt playmat at night: everything cut from felt with stitched edges and fibres, Dobbin in a tartan gown, the bin in blue wire mesh, and every path a strand of glowing yarn.
Seven night blues and one cyan, which is exactly what a firefly in the dark looks like. White is for stitches, Dobbin's moustache, and the signs.

A hushed campfire shanty, the kind you sing under your breath after lights-out, on a squeezebox and a fiddle, in the Japanese in-sen scale (D, E♭, G, A, C). It fills out as the park does. Every pluck and bell in the game is on the same five notes.
Everything is OVERHEARD at the taps, in capital letters, by people who were definitely not looking. Dobbin gets a few lines. The bin gets a few more, all of them confident.

rolls.value: an obscure observance: Take a Hike Day (17 November)
rolls.became: One of the silly swaps: a Take a Hike Day leaflet from the noticeboard, stuck to the back of Dobbin's dressing gown. Everyone he shouts at gets to read it as he walks away.

outro: The bin was right about one thing: it never missed.
